The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it.

Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

You are the procurement team of Hollerau Pumpenwerke, a fictional German pump maker, and the inbox is full: a foundry wants +9.5 %, a framework contract expires, a new pump needs three quotes. Build an **AI buyer agent** that reads the company's data, negotiates by e-mail with our supplier bots, and closes the best total deal, or walks away. Practise all weekend against our hosted suppliers. On Sunday at 12:00 a Live Final on hidden cases ranks every team. This repo holds everything you need: the brief, the API docs, a Python starter kit and the data package. Bring your own LLM, any provider; we run the suppliers. ## Start in 15 minutes You need Python 3.12, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and git. 1. **Apply.** Open **https://arena.tacto.ai/apply** and enter your team name and a contact e-mail. Tip: start the name with one emoji, it shows on the big screen. 2. **Show your match code at the Tacto desk.** We approve. 3. **Copy your key.** It appears **once** on the page you applied on; then press "Got the key". One key per team. Lost it? We reset it at the desk. 4. **Run the four commands.** ```bash git clone https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit.git cd negotiation-arena-kit/starter-kit cp .env.example .env # paste your key: ARENA_API_KEY=... uv sync --all-extras # install uv run arena me # your team and its practice quota uv run arena play case:P01 # the naive example agent negotiates one practice case uv run arena board # your team on the practice leaderboard ``` `arena play` prints the deal, your score and a replay link: every e-mail and the supplier's reasons in words. Read it, improve your agent, play again. Next steps, the LLM agent and your own agent: [starter-kit/README.md](starter-kit/README.md). ## Links | What | Where | |---|---| | Apply for your key | https://arena.tacto.ai/apply | | Brief: story, task, score, rules | [brief/brief.md](brief/brief.md) | | API docs | [brief/api.md](brief/api.md) | | Starter kit: client, example agents, Live Final runner, local simulator, MCP server | [starter-kit/](starter-kit/) | | Submission and pitch | [brief/submission.md](brief/submission.md) | | Practice build page: every team's quota, records and highlights | https://arena.tacto.ai/live | | Live Final results, team by team and case by case | https://arena.tacto.ai/results | | Questions | Discord https://discord.gg/hPwFfbWRV · the Tacto table | ## The weekend at a glance | When | What | |---|---| | Sat 10:00 | Kickoff and reveal: brief, data, kit and practice arena go live | | Sat 12:00-13:00 | **Deep dive**, ground floor (room on the signs): data, API, kit, Q&A. Bring a laptop. Challenge selection closes 13:00 | | Sat afternoon | Office hours at the Tacto table. Practice all weekend: 200 sessions per team per 24 hours | | Sat evening | We post on Discord when Tacto goes offline for the night | | Sun 08:00 | **New market data.** Run `uv run arena data` again; hidden cases may cite it | | Sun 09:00 | Pre-flight: one practice case through your final setup | | Sun 12:00 | **Code freeze**, submit on ehl.gg. **Live Final**: five waves, 8 minutes each, every team at once | | Sun 13:00 | **Top 10 pitch** to the Tacto jury: 5 minutes + 2 minutes of questions | | Sun 14:30 | Track winners and the two finalists announced | | Sun 15:30 | Grand Final pitches (AudiMax) | | Sun 16:30 | Awards | ## Rules that matter - **No human in the loop** during the Live Final. They are for you, not for your agent. - **One key per team.** No attacks on the service or on other teams. - Everything else counts, including weaknesses you find in our suppliers. Every replay is open to the jury. All rules: [brief, section 7](brief/brief.md#7-rules). ## What to submit on ehl.gg by Sun 12:00 - **Your repo** with the agent and a README that says how to run it, and the **commit hash** your agent runs in the final. The jury and tum.ai must be able to open it. - **A short description** of your approach. - **Slides** for the pitch. The top 10 pitch from 13:00. Tacto · AI for industrial procurement · EHL Grand Finale 2026, Garching

# brief - `brief.md` - the participant brief (max. 4 pages) - `api.md` - the HTTP API reference - `submission.md` - what to submit on Sunday, and how the pitch works # Tacto Negotiation Arena - Participant brief > **Build an AI buyer agent that negotiates by e-mail with tough, realistic industrial suppliers, > gets the best total deal - and can explain how it got there.** ## 1. The story You are the procurement team of **Hollerau Pumpenwerke GmbH**, a fictional German pump maker: centrifugal pumps for buildings, water and industry, about €250M revenue, 900 people, one plant in Bavaria. Your team buys the parts of the pump line - castings, machined parts, sheet metal, seals, motors, fasteners, stainless bar - from about 45 suppliers. Today is **30 September 2026**, and the inbox is full: a foundry announces +9.5% on volute casings "due to energy and wages", a framework contract expires, a new pump series needs three quotes, a supplier with a red scorecard has to fix its quality. You answer the way buyers do: by e-mail. On the other side sit our **supplier bots**, each with a small team of **roles** behind it - the sales rep or owner who writes to you, a boss who must approve bigger moves, and engineering, quality, logistics, finance or legal, who answer their topics and attach documents. Tacto is the AI for industrial procurement: it gives procurement teams the intelligence to source every part at the best possible terms with minimal effort. Your company runs on that kind of data - orders, deliveries, invoices, contracts, scorecards, market indices, should-cost estimates, notes from supplier calls. Your job is to build the agent that turns this data into better deals. (In Tacto's product, agents such as the Defender Agent or the Sourcing Agent do parts of this job.) ## 2. The task Each **case** is one negotiation: a trigger (a letter, an expiring contract, an RFQ), your case file (need, goal, rates, must-haves, your alternative) and one to three supplier bots. Your **buyer agent** 1. **prepares** - reads the case file and mines the data package; 2. **negotiates by e-mail** - plain-language messages with up to three **term sheets** (alternative packages), the data IDs your arguments rest on, and attachments if you like; 3. **closes** - accepts one supplier term sheet, or walks away. **How a supplier decides.** Each supplier is a company with its own economics and a person at the desk - a family foundry that remembers how you treated it, a group with an approval ladder, a job shop that needs cash and work, a near-monopolist that barely moves. Its hard limits come from its own situation: it never sells below its cost floor, bigger moves need the boss's approval, data you cite is checked by ID, and it gives nothing without a move from you. Inside those limits it decides as that person would - reading your whole e-mail: the term sheets, the data, and what you signal (questions, arguments, threats, appreciation, urgency). It reacts to tone and relationship as people do; padding does not buy price. **Data is not automatically rewarded.** True data can disarm a supplier ("we didn't know that") - or meet "that's not our reality", because something else weighs more for it right now. The traces are in the data: call notes, letters, news, the remarks on its quotes. The skill is reading the supplier, not stacking evidence - and finding the trade it wants: a supplier short of cash may care more about when it is paid than about the price; one that cannot touch its list price may still move on other terms. ## 3. What you get (Sat 10:00) | What | Where | |---|---| | This brief, the API docs (`api.md`) and the submission guide (`submission.md`) | `https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit`, folder `brief/` | | **Data package v1**: CSV, the same data as SQLite, `facts.json` (every citable ID with the values the arena checks), contracts, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes - the data behind all 19 practice cases | `https://arena.tacto.ai/v1/data/package.zip`, or the repo's `data/` | | **Practice arena**: 10 hosted practice cases, picked so every case type shows up; a replay after every case; practice leaderboard; a **sandbox** with 3 demo suppliers | `https://arena.tacto.ai` with your team's key - apply at `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply` (below) | | **Starter kit**: Python client, a naive agent, an LLM agent that writes e-mails and reads the attached documents, the Live Final runner, an MCP server over the data, `arena-sim` - the API on your laptop | the repo's `starter-kit/` - first agent on the board in 15 minutes | You bring your own LLM access; we only run the suppliers. Data and docs are CC BY 4.0, code MIT. **Your key - one per team.** Open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a contact e-mail, and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once we approve, the key appears **once** on that page: copy it, press "Got the key". Only that page shows it; lost it - we reset it. Tip: your team name may start with one emoji - it shows on the big screen (optional; nothing offensive). **Practice quota: 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours.** `GET /v1/me` shows what you have used and when it frees up. The build page `https://arena.tacto.ai/live` shows every team's quota use, practice records and highlights from Sat 10:00 to Sun 12:00. **`arena-sim`** speaks the arena's API exactly, with one plain scripted supplier: get your plumbing right there. It teaches the contract, not the suppliers - and we don't hand out our suppliers. Want a local opponent? Build your own supplier simulator from the public data: thinking into how real suppliers act is part of the challenge. **The learning loop:** play a practice case, read your exact score and its cost breakdown, open the replay - every e-mail and the supplier's reasons in words, as a real supplier would give them - improve your agent, play again. Your best score per practice case counts. ## 4. The data The buyer's world: supplier and part master data; three years of orders, goods receipts, invoices and payments; quality notifications and quarterly scorecards (on-time delivery, PPM); framework contracts and clauses; past RFQs and quotes; forecasts; supplier intel and news; past negotiations, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes; should-cost estimates; spend down to the long tail; and monthly market indices (real public series, frozen at 2026-09-30). - **Every fact you can cite has an ID** `:[@period]`, e.g. `po:4500010001-10`, `idx:PPI-C2451@2026-08`, `sc:70110@2026Q3`, `ctr:4600070110#3.1`, `doc:…`. - What moves a supplier is in the data - some of it only in the notes and e-mails. Some notes are just noise. The company and its suppliers are fictional. - **Sunday 08:00: a second release** - market news, supplier letters and a memo from early October (`GET /v1/data` lists it). Hidden cases may cite its facts. Your agent should read it. ## 5. How a negotiation works - **Round 0:** every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once, with a quote PDF. - **Your message:** subject, body, up to 3 term sheets (each with a value for every negotiable field), the data IDs you rely on (IDs written in the body count too), optional text attachments. - **The supplier answers by e-mail:** the role in charge writes; its standing term sheet; a status - `open`, `final_offer` (push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms; you still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid`; signals (reply delay, quote validity); fields it left out; and how each data argument checked out. A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**; its time never counts against your 60 seconds. - **Only you close a deal**, by accepting a supplier's standing term sheet. In **RFQ cases** 2-3 suppliers run in parallel threads; accepting one ends the case. - **Limits:** a round limit per thread (default 10 messages) and **60 seconds per message**, counted from the supplier's reply. A late message counts as a timeout: your last offer repeated, the supplier's patience drops; three in a row, or one after the last round, end the thread. - **Unstated terms default to the supplier's standard terms** - listed in its quote PDF. **Documents** are rendered from the supplier's data, never invented: the quote PDF (read it before you accept), a cost breakdown XLSX (ask; an open supplier sends one), an 8D report (quality), a delivery schedule XLSX (logistics), and the order confirmation at the deal. **What counts:** **term sheets bind** - nothing else. **Data you cite is checked**: the reply says `verified`, `contradicted` (a wrong figure or an unknown ID - it costs trust), `irrelevant` or `duplicate`; whether a true argument moves the supplier, and how far, is the supplier's business. **What you write is understood** - and has consequences, as it would with a person. ## 6. What to hand in for the Tacto track, and how the pitch works. Deadline: **Sunday 12:00 on ehl.gg**.

## What to submit

1. **Your repo:** the agent and a README that says how to run it (setup, the environment variables it
   needs, without values, and the command). Put the **commit hash** your agent runs in the final into
   the description. The jury and tum.ai must be able to open the repo; tum.ai runs a code agent over
   every submission.
2. **A short description** of your approach: how your agent prepares, what it reads in the data, how
   it decides what to offer, and when it closes or walks away.
3. **Slides** for the pitch. The top 10 present them from 13:00.

Keep every key out of the repo: no `.env`, no LLM key, no arena key.

## At 12:00 your agent is already running

The code freeze and the Live Final start together, so start your agent before 12:00 and leave it
running:

```bash
uv run arena run --set final --agent llm --parallel 10
```

Or your own runner that polls `GET /v1/cases?set=final`. The kit's runner waits for wave 1, plays each
wave's cases in parallel within the 8-minute cap and stops after the fifth wave. From 12:00 there is no
human in the loop, and your agent must not read `/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard` or `/results`.
We check the top 10 for pushes after the freeze.

Checklist for 11:30:

- The machine and network you use for the final; one practice case went through it at the 09:00
  pre-flight.
- `uv run arena data` ran after 08:00, so the Sunday release sits next to the package.
- `uv run arena me` answers with your team: the key works.
- LLM credits and rate limits for about an hour of parallel play.
- The runner is started and logs to a file; the laptop is on power and does not sleep.

## The pitch

- **The top 10:** the ten teams with the most points after the five waves.
- **5 minutes pitch + 2 minutes of questions**, from 13:00. tum.ai keeps the time; the slot does not
  stretch.
- **Every replay is open to the jury.** After the final, each case on https://arena.tacto.ai/results
  links to its replay. Pick one negotiation and walk us through it.
- Questions to expect: Why did your agent write that? Would it have worked on a real supplier? What
  did your agent learn about suppliers, and from where?
- ⟦Q2: how the Live Final score and the jury combine for places 1-3, and the jury criteria⟧
# Tacto Negotiation Arena - starter kit

A Python client for the arena API, two example buyer agents that negotiate by e-mail, helpers that
read the suppliers' documents and price a term sheet, a runner that plays many cases in parallel,
`arena-sim` - a local simulator of the arena's API - and a read-only MCP server over the data
package. Read the brief first
(`../brief/brief.md`); the full API is in `../brief/api.md`. Code: MIT.

## Quickstart - first agent on the board in 15 minutes

You need Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

**1. Get your team's key** (one per team): open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a
contact e-mail, and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once an organiser approves,
the key appears **once** on that page - copy it and press "Got the key". Only that page (or its
link) shows it; lost it → ask the organisers to reset it. Keep it out of git.

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv sync --all-extras            # 2. install
cp .env.example .env            # 3. put ARENA_URL and your key (ARENA_API_KEY) into .env
uv run arena me                 # 4. your team and its practice quota
uv run arena cases              # 5. the practice cases (the 10 hosted ones are playable)
uv run arena play case:P01 -v   # 6. the naive agent negotiates one case
uv run arena board              # 7. you are on the practice leaderboard
```

Is the arena up? `curl $ARENA_URL/health`.

Step 6 prints the deal, your total cost `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, the case score,
and a **replay link**: every e-mail and the supplier's reasons for each move, in words. That is
the learning loop - play a practice case, read the replay, improve your agent, play
again. In practice your best score per case counts, so play a case again whenever your agent improves.
**Quota:** 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours. `arena play` and `arena run` print
how many are left; `arena run` plays only the hosted practice cases and stops starting new ones
once the quota is used up (a `429` there does not go away by retrying). Plan your runs.

**Now the LLM agent.** Download the data (`ARENA_DATA=data/package` in `.env`), choose a model in
`.env` (your own key), then:

```bash
uv run arena data                                          # unpacks data/package (and the Sunday release once public)
uv run arena play case:P01 --agent llm -v
uv run arena run --set practice --agent llm --parallel 8   # every hosted practice case, 8 at a time
uv run arena play case:D02 -v                              # the sandbox: 3 demo suppliers, no board
```

**Sunday 08:00:** run `arena data` again - it adds `data/release-sunday` (new news, letters, a
memo). `DataPackage` merges its facts and documents automatically; hidden cases may cite them.

## Hello World (local, 3 commands)

No key yet? Play a whole case against the local simulator - no network, no quota, no LLM costs.
The simulator's supplier is a plain script; the real ones are on arena.tacto.ai. After
`uv sync --all-extras` (step 2 above):

```bash
# terminal 1: the simulator (--data is optional: leave it out until you have run `arena data`)
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package
# terminal 2: a simulator key, then the naive agent plays case:S01
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Hello World" sim                  # prints an api_key
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 ARENA_API_KEY=<the api_key> uv run arena play case:S01 -v
```

It prints the deal, `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, the score and a replay link - open it
in your browser: the result on top, then every e-mail of the negotiation.

## Try it by hand (Postman, curl)

Feel the API before you put a model in front of it. On the real arena (practice and sandbox) the
60-second rule applies: three late replies in a row end the thread - too fast for typing. **By
hand, use the simulator first**, without the clock:

```bash
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package           # data/package from `arena data`; --data is optional
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Team Name" sim   # prints a simulator api_key
export SIM=http://127.0.0.1:8000 KEY=<the api_key>
```

Every call sends `X-API-Key: <key>`; every `POST` also `Content-Type: application/json` and a
fresh `X-Move-Id` (any unique string - the same id again returns the same answer). In Postman:
those headers, the body as raw JSON.

```bash
# 1. the cases: case:S01 has one supplier, sup:70270, and the negotiable fields unit_price, payment_days
curl -s "$SIM/v1/cases?set=practice" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"

# 2. open a session: the reply carries session_id (sim1 on a fresh simulator) and each supplier's quote e-mail
curl -s -X POST "$SIM/v1/sessions" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Move-Id: open-1" -d '{"case_id": "case:S01"}'

# 3. the supplier's opening e-mail: its term sheet (offer:70270-0) and the quote PDF to fetch
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"

# 4. your e-mail with an offer: the reply is the supplier's answer (status, term_sheets, claim_results)
curl -s -X POST "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270/messages" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Move-Id: msg-1" \
  -d '{"message": {"subject": "Adapter piece HI", "body": "Thank you for your quote. We offer 15.50 EUR at 60 days.",
       "term_sheets": [{"terms": {"unit_price": 15.5, "payment_days": 60}}]}}'

# 5. read the reply in the thread, and the session state
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"
```

To close, send `{"message": {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": "offer:70270-1"}}}` (the
term sheet you take) or `{"message": {"action": {"type": "walk_away"}}}` to the same `messages` path;
the answer carries the result and score. The quote PDF: `GET $SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/attachments/att:70270-0-quote`.
The same calls work on the arena (`https://arena.tacto.ai`, your team's key, a practice case) - with
the clock running.

## The Live Final: waves, in parallel, within the cap

The final comes in 5 themed waves. A wave holds several hidden cases that appear when the host
starts it; play them all in parallel (up to 10 open sessions per key). Each wave has a hard
cap - **8 minutes** (the host may extend one) - and what is still open then ends without a deal.
Start the runner before the first wave and leave it running:

```bash
uv run arena run --set final --agent llm --parallel 10
```

It polls `GET /v1/cases?set=final`, plays every case of a new wave at once (one agent per case),
closes each case **90 seconds before its wave's cap** (read from the wave's `seconds_left`, so an
extension counts) - earlier if a round in that case took longer
(`play.closing_move`: the cheapest standing term
sheet that keeps the must-haves and beats your alternative, else walk away) and stops after the
fifth wave has closed. If it crashes, start it again: it picks up the sessions it had started.
In Python: `play_waves(client, new_agent)`. It reads only your own cases and sessions - during
the final your agent must not read the leaderboard, the screen or the event feed (`arena board`
is for you, not for the agent).

A supplier's reply can take up to about a minute; its time never counts against your 60 seconds,
and the client waits up to 180 seconds for a reply. The client paces itself below the
limit of 10 calls per second and retries dropped connections with the same `X-Move-Id`, so a
retry never sends a message twice. Rehearse with `arena run --set practice --parallel 10` (it counts against your quota) before
Sunday, from the machine and network you will use: every case should end well inside 8 minutes.

## Your own agent

An agent is any object with `decide(case, threads) -> {"supplier_id": …, "message": {…}}`.
`threads` holds every e-mail so far per supplier, oldest first; supplier attachments come with
their text under `"text"`. The message is an e-mail - subject, body, up to 3 term sheets - or an
action that closes the case:

```python
from arena_kit import ArenaClient, RemoteTable, complete_offer, play, total_cost
from arena_kit.docs import standard_terms
from arena_kit.play import latest, live_threads, standing


class Haggler:
    def decide(self, case, threads):
        sid = live_threads(threads)[0]
        events = threads[sid]
        sheet_id, terms = standing(events)  # the supplier's standing term sheet
        std = standard_terms(events)  # from its quote PDF: what closes if a field is missing
        if latest(events)["status"] in ("agreed", "final_offer"):
            return {
                "supplier_id": sid,
                "message": {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": sheet_id}},
            }
        ask = complete_offer(case, {**terms, "unit_price": terms["unit_price"] * 0.97})
        print("their C:", total_cost(case, terms, std), "ours:", total_cost(case, ask))
        return {
            "supplier_id": sid,
            "message": {
                "subject": case["title"],
                "body": "Thank you for your quote. Could you send us a cost breakdown?",
                "term_sheets": [{"terms": ask}],
            },
        }


print(play(RemoteTable(ArenaClient()), "case:P01", Haggler()))
```

| Module | What |
|---|---|
| `client.py` | `ArenaClient`: one method per endpoint (messages, threads, attachments, back office, `me`, ...); paced, safe retries; `practice_remaining` |
| `play.py` | `play()`, `play_all()`, `play_waves()` (the Live Final); `RemoteTable` - the hosted arena (practice, sandbox, final) |
| `cost.py` | the published cost function C with the category goal's rates, `supplier_value` for the relationship term, must-haves, term-sheet completion |
| `docs.py` | supplier documents to text (PDF, XLSX); a quote PDF to its offered, standard and fixed terms |
| `data.py` | the data package and the Sunday release: `facts.json`, read-only SQL, lookup by ID, documents, cases |
| `agents/naive.py` | anchors 10 % low, splits the difference, accepts early - the baseline |
| `agents/llm.py` | the model writes the e-mail and the term sheets from the case and the data it points to; code computes C, reads the documents, removes IDs that do not exist, and refuses bad accepts |
| `sim.py` | `arena-sim`: the public API on your machine, with one plain scripted supplier (below) |
| `mcp_server.py` | the MCP server below |

The LLM agent is a starting point, not a winner: it sees only what the case file points to.
Finding the data that moves a supplier is your job - the worked example below shows one way for
one kind of argument. Ideas beyond it: mine the notes and e-mails, read the suppliers' signals and
documents, send two or three term sheets to learn what a supplier values, ask its roles the right
questions, keep RFQ threads alive in parallel, and never leak urgency, a budget or a missing
alternative.

**Strategic and bottleneck cases** (`category_goal` `stabilise` or `secure_supply`) charge C for a
deal that leaves the supplier below a sustainable margin. Pass your estimate of the supplier to
price it - without one, `total_cost` leaves the term out:

```python
supplier = {"full_cost": 128.0, "interest_rate": 0.12, "standard": std}  # your estimate
total_cost(case, terms, std, supplier)
```

## Worked example: cite an index (case P01)

Brandlhuber, a foundry, announces +9.5 % on volute casings and blames energy and wages. Does the
data agree? `DataPackage` reads the package (the MCP server below gives an LLM the same access):

```python
from arena_kit.data import DataPackage

pkg = DataPackage("data/package")
# 1. What drives this part's cost? The category team's estimate:
pkg.query("SELECT series_id, weight FROM cost_drivers WHERE part_id = 'part:310010'")
# -> PPI-C241 (iron and steel) 0.26, PPI-D351 (electric power) 0.06, LCI-C (labour) 0.32
# 2. The letter blames energy: read the electricity producer price index for the last year.
rows = pkg.query(
    "SELECT id, month, value FROM index_values WHERE series_id = 'PPI-D351' AND month >= '2025-08' ORDER BY month"
)
# 3. Compute the change yourself - two months of one series, at most 12 months apart,
#    ending within the last 12 months of the data.
a, b = rows[0], rows[-1]
change = (b["value"] / a["value"] - 1) * 100
# 4. One sentence: the figure next to both IDs.
print(f"Electricity producer prices changed {change:+.1f}% from {a['month']} to {b['month']} ({a['id']}, {b['id']}).")
# -> Electricity producer prices changed -3.7% from 2025-08 to 2026-08
#    (idx:PPI-D351@2025-08, idx:PPI-D351@2026-08).
```

Put that sentence into your e-mail and read `claim_results` in the reply: `verified` (the figure
matches the data), `irrelevant` (true, but not about this supplier's costs, or the window is too
old) or `contradicted` (a wrong figure - it costs trust). Whether it moves the price, and how far,
is the supplier's business - a true figure may disarm one supplier and leave the next cold; the
replay shows what it made of it. Which series matter to which
supplier, which window, and what else in the data speaks for you - that is up to your agent.

## Choosing a model

`LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic` uses the Anthropic SDK (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`); `LLM_PROVIDER=openai` talks
to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_API_KEY`) - OpenAI, Mistral, Groq, a local
Ollama (`http://localhost:11434/v1`) and many more. Or pass your own `complete(system, user) -> str`
to `LLMAgent`. Each message must arrive within **60 seconds** of the supplier's reply: prefer a
fast model or low effort, and do heavy research before you open a session. If the model fails or times out, the agent falls
back to the naive move instead of losing the case.

## Offline: arena-sim, the contract simulator

```bash
uv run arena-sim serve --data /path/to/data/package   # http://127.0.0.1:8000, event code "sim"
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Team Name" sim   # a simulator key
```

`arena register` exists for the simulator only: it hands out its own keys, which work nowhere
else. The arena's key comes from `/apply` (step 1).

`arena-sim` speaks the arena's public API exactly - paths, fields, statuses, error codes, limits,
the 60-second rule, quote PDFs and cost-breakdown XLSX files in the arena's format, RFQs with
parallel threads, leaderboard and replay JSON - with three example cases (`case:S01`-`S03`). Point
your agent at it to get the plumbing right without a network or a rate limit to worry about.
`--no-clock` switches the 60-second rule off for trying it by hand (above); without it the clock
runs, as on the arena. The first line it prints says which.

Its supplier is a deliberately plain script and **not** how the arena's suppliers behave: it opens
10 % above your current price, concedes a fixed 2 % per term sheet down to 90 %, agrees when you
meet its price, sends a final offer from round 5 and walks if you push after that; cited data is
only checked for existence. **The simulator teaches the contract; the real suppliers think for
themselves** - practise against them in the hosted arena and its sandbox (`--set sandbox`). We
don't hand out our suppliers: for a local opponent, build your own supplier simulator from the
public data - how would a foundry owner with a full order book answer your e-mail?
`starter-kit/Dockerfile` runs the simulator as a container. `uv run pytest` runs the kit's contract
tests against it; set `ARENA_TEST_URL` and `ARENA_TEST_KEY` to run them against a hosted arena too.

## MCP server over the data

A local, read-only MCP server (stdio) lets an MCP-capable agent or chat client explore the data
package itself. Six tools: `list_tables`, `query` (SELECT only, max 200 rows), `lookup` (the fact
behind a citable ID), `list_ids` (e.g. every month of one index series), `read_document`,
`get_case`.

```bash
uv run arena mcp --data /path/to/data/package   # speaks MCP on stdin/stdout
```

Add it to a client, e.g. Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add arena-data -- uv run --directory /path/to/starter-kit arena mcp --data /path/to/data/package
```

or any client with an `mcpServers` config:

```json
{"mcpServers": {"arena-data": {"command": "uv", "args": ["run", "--directory", "/path/to/starter-kit",
  "arena", "mcp", "--data", "/path/to/data/package"]}}}
```

## Good to know

- **60 s per message**, per thread. A late message counts as a timeout (your last offer repeated);
  `play()` reads the supplier's answer and goes on.
- **Invalid messages cost nothing**: `422` and no round used. `409` means the thread or case has
  ended, or you were late.
- **Your key is your team's.** Keep `.env` out of git.
- Tests: `uv run pytest`. Lint: `uv run ruff check .`

contact e-mail, and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once an organiser approves,
the key appears **once** on that page - copy it and press "Got the key". Only that page (or its
link) shows it; lost it → ask the organisers to reset it. Keep it out of git.

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv sync --all-extras            # 2. install
cp .env.example .env            # 3. put ARENA_URL and your key (ARENA_API_KEY) into .env
uv run arena me                 # 4. your team and its practice quota
uv run arena cases              # 5. the practice cases (the 10 hosted ones are playable)
uv run arena play case:P01 -v   # 6. the naive agent negotiates one case
uv run arena board              # 7. you are on the practice leaderboard
```

Is the arena up? `curl $ARENA_URL/health`.

Step 6 prints the deal, your total cost `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, the case score,
and a **replay link**: every e-mail and the supplier's reasons for each move, in words. That is
the learning loop - play a practice case, read the replay, improve your agent, play
again. In practice your best score per case counts, so play a case again whenever your agent improves.
**Quota:** 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours. `arena play` and `arena run` print
how many are left; `arena run` plays only the hosted practice cases and stops starting new ones
once the quota is used up (a `429` there does not go away by retrying). Plan your runs.

**Now the LLM agent.** Download the data (`ARENA_DATA=data/package` in `.env`), choose a model in
`.env` (your own key), then:

```bash
uv run arena data                                          # unpacks data/package (and the Sunday release once public)
uv run arena play case:P01 --agent llm -v
uv run arena run --set practice --agent llm --parallel 8   # every hosted practice case, 8 at a time
uv run arena play case:D02 -v                              # the sandbox: 3 demo suppliers, no board
```

**Sunday 08:00:** run `arena data` again - it adds `data/release-sunday` (new news, letters, a
memo). `DataPackage` merges its facts and documents automatically; hidden cases may cite them.

## Hello World (local, 3 commands)

No key yet? Play a whole case against the local simulator - no network, no quota, no LLM costs.
The simulator's supplier is a plain script; the real ones are on arena.tacto.ai. After
`uv sync --all-extras` (step 2 above):

```bash
# terminal 1: the simulator (--data is optional: leave it out until you have run `arena data`)
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package
# terminal 2: a simulator key, then the naive agent plays case:S01
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Hello World" sim                  # prints an api_key
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 ARENA_API_KEY=<the api_key> uv run arena play case:S01 -v
```

It prints the deal, `c_deal` against `c_open` and `c_best`, the score and a replay link - open it
in your browser: the result on top, then every e-mail of the negotiation.

## Try it by hand (Postman, curl)

Feel the API before you put a model in front of it. On the real arena (practice and sandbox) the
60-second rule applies: three late replies in a row end the thread - too fast for typing. **By
hand, use the simulator first**, without the clock:

```bash
uv run arena-sim serve --no-clock --data data/package           # data/package from `arena data`; --data is optional
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Team Name" sim   # prints a simulator api_key
export SIM=http://127.0.0.1:8000 KEY=<the api_key>
```

Every call sends `X-API-Key: <key>`; every `POST` also `Content-Type: application/json` and a
fresh `X-Move-Id` (any unique string - the same id again returns the same answer). In Postman:
those headers, the body as raw JSON.

```bash
# 1. the cases: case:S01 has one supplier, sup:70270, and the negotiable fields unit_price, payment_days
curl -s "$SIM/v1/cases?set=practice" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"

# 2. open a session: the reply carries session_id (sim1 on a fresh simulator) and each supplier's quote e-mail
curl -s -X POST "$SIM/v1/sessions" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Move-Id: open-1" -d '{"case_id": "case:S01"}'

# 3. the supplier's opening e-mail: its term sheet (offer:70270-0) and the quote PDF to fetch
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"

# 4. your e-mail with an offer: the reply is the supplier's answer (status, term_sheets, claim_results)
curl -s -X POST "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270/messages" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Move-Id: msg-1" \
  -d '{"message": {"subject": "Adapter piece HI", "body": "Thank you for your quote. We offer 15.50 EUR at 60 days.",
       "term_sheets": [{"terms": {"unit_price": 15.5, "payment_days": 60}}]}}'

# 5. read the reply in the thread, and the session state
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/threads/sup:70270" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"
curl -s "$SIM/v1/sessions/sim1" -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"
```

To close, send `{"message": {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": "offer:70270-1"}}}` (the
term sheet you take) or `{"message": {"action": {"type": "walk_away"}}}` to the same `messages` path;
the answer carries the result and score. The quote PDF: `GET $SIM/v1/sessions/sim1/attachments/att:70270-0-quote`.
The same calls work on the arena (`https://arena.tacto.ai`, your team's key, a practice case) - with
the clock running.

## The Live Final: waves, in parallel, within the cap

The final comes in 5 themed waves. A wave holds several hidden cases that appear when the host
starts it; play them all in parallel (up to 10 open sessions per key). Each wave has a hard
cap - **8 minutes** (the host may extend one) - and what is still open then ends without a deal.
Start the runner before the first wave and leave it running:

```bash
uv run arena run --set final --agent llm --parallel 10
```

It polls `GET /v1/cases?set=final`, plays every case of a new wave at once (one agent per case),
closes each case **90 seconds before its wave's cap** (read from the wave's `seconds_left`, so an
extension counts) - earlier if a round in that case took longer
(`play.closing_move`: the cheapest standing term
sheet that keeps the must-haves and beats your alternative, else walk away) and stops after the
fifth wave has closed. If it crashes, start it again: it picks up the sessions it had started.
In Python: `play_waves(client, new_agent)`. It reads only your own cases and sessions - during
the final your agent must not read the leaderboard, the screen or the event feed (`arena board`
is for you, not for the agent).

A supplier's reply can take up to about a minute; its time never counts against your 60 seconds,
and the client waits up to 180 seconds for a reply. The client paces itself below the
limit of 10 calls per second and retries dropped connections with the same `X-Move-Id`, so a
retry never sends a message twice. Rehearse with `arena run --set practice --parallel 10` (it counts against your quota) before
Sunday, from the machine and network you will use: every case should end well inside 8 minutes.

## Your own agent

An agent is any object with `decide(case, threads) -> {"supplier_id": …, "message": {…}}`.
`threads` holds every e-mail so far per supplier, oldest first; supplier attachments come with
their text under `"text"`. The message is an e-mail - subject, body, up to 3 term sheets - or an
action that closes the case:

```python
from arena_kit import ArenaClient, RemoteTable, complete_offer, play, total_cost
from arena_kit.docs import standard_terms
from arena_kit.play import latest, live_threads, standing


class Haggler:
    def decide(self, case, threads):
        sid = live_threads(threads)[0]
        events = threads[sid]
        sheet_id, terms = standing(events)  # the supplier's standing term sheet
        std = standard_terms(events)  # from its quote PDF: what closes if a field is missing
        if latest(events)["status"] in ("agreed", "final_offer"):
            return {
                "supplier_id": sid,
                "message": {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": sheet_id}},
            }
        ask = complete_offer(case, {**terms, "unit_price": terms["unit_price"] * 0.97})
        print("their C:", total_cost(case, terms, std), "ours:", total_cost(case, ask))
        return {
            "supplier_id": sid,
            "message": {
                "subject": case["title"],
                "body": "Thank you for your quote. Could you send us a cost breakdown?",
                "term_sheets": [{"terms": ask}],
            },
        }


print(play(RemoteTable(ArenaClient()), "case:P01", Haggler()))
```

| Module | What |
|---|---|
| `client.py` | `ArenaClient`: one method per endpoint (messages, threads, attachments, back office, `me`, ...); paced, safe retries; `practice_remaining` |
| `play.py` | `play()`, `play_all()`, `play_waves()` (the Live Final); `RemoteTable` - the hosted arena (practice, sandbox, final) |
| `cost.py` | the published cost function C with the category goal's rates, `supplier_value` for the relationship term, must-haves, term-sheet completion |
| `docs.py` | supplier documents to text (PDF, XLSX); a quote PDF to its offered, standard and fixed terms |
| `data.py` | the data package and the Sunday release: `facts.json`, read-only SQL, lookup by ID, documents, cases |
| `agents/naive.py` | anchors 10 % low, splits the difference, accepts early - the baseline |
| `agents/llm.py` | the model writes the e-mail and the term sheets from the case and the data it points to; code computes C, reads the documents, removes IDs that do not exist, and refuses bad accepts |
| `sim.py` | `arena-sim`: the public API on your machine, with one plain scripted supplier (below) |
| `mcp_server.py` | the MCP server below |

The LLM agent is a starting point, not a winner: it sees only what the case file points to.
Finding the data that moves a supplier is your job - the worked example below shows one way for
one kind of argument. Ideas beyond it: mine the notes and e-mails, read the suppliers' signals and
documents, send two or three term sheets to learn what a supplier values, ask its roles the right
questions, keep RFQ threads alive in parallel, and never leak urgency, a budget or a missing
alternative.

**Strategic and bottleneck cases** (`category_goal` `stabilise` or `secure_supply`) charge C for a
deal that leaves the supplier below a sustainable margin. Pass your estimate of the supplier to
price it - without one, `total_cost` leaves the term out:

```python
supplier = {"full_cost": 128.0, "interest_rate": 0.12, "standard": std}  # your estimate
total_cost(case, terms, std, supplier)
```

## Worked example: cite an index (case P01)

Brandlhuber, a foundry, announces +9.5 % on volute casings and blames energy and wages. Does the
data agree? `DataPackage` reads the package (the MCP server below gives an LLM the same access):

```python
from arena_kit.data import DataPackage

pkg = DataPackage("data/package")
# 1. What drives this part's cost? The category team's estimate:
pkg.query("SELECT series_id, weight FROM cost_drivers WHERE part_id = 'part:310010'")
# -> PPI-C241 (iron and steel) 0.26, PPI-D351 (electric power) 0.06, LCI-C (labour) 0.32
# 2. The letter blames energy: read the electricity producer price index for the last year.
rows = pkg.query(
    "SELECT id, month, value FROM index_values WHERE series_id = 'PPI-D351' AND month >= '2025-08' ORDER BY month"
)
# 3. Compute the change yourself - two months of one series, at most 12 months apart,
#    ending within the last 12 months of the data.
a, b = rows[0], rows[-1]
change = (b["value"] / a["value"] - 1) * 100
# 4. One sentence: the figure next to both IDs.
print(f"Electricity producer prices changed {change:+.1f}% from {a['month']} to {b['month']} ({a['id']}, {b['id']}).")
# -> Electricity producer prices changed -3.7% from 2025-08 to 2026-08
#    (idx:PPI-D351@2025-08, idx:PPI-D351@2026-08).
```

Put that sentence into your e-mail and read `claim_results` in the reply: `verified` (the figure
matches the data), `irrelevant` (true, but not about this supplier's costs, or the window is too
old) or `contradicted` (a wrong figure - it costs trust). Whether it moves the price, and how far,
is the supplier's business - a true figure may disarm one supplier and leave the next cold; the
replay shows what it made of it. Which series matter to which
supplier, which window, and what else in the data speaks for you - that is up to your agent.

## Choosing a model

`LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic` uses the Anthropic SDK (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`); `LLM_PROVIDER=openai` talks
to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_API_KEY`) - OpenAI, Mistral, Groq, a local
Ollama (`http://localhost:11434/v1`) and many more. Or pass your own `complete(system, user) -> str`
to `LLMAgent`. Each message must arrive within **60 seconds** of the supplier's reply: prefer a
fast model or low effort, and do heavy research before you open a session. If the model fails or times out, the agent falls
back to the naive move instead of losing the case.

## Offline: arena-sim, the contract simulator

```bash
uv run arena-sim serve --data /path/to/data/package   # http://127.0.0.1:8000, event code "sim"
ARENA_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000 uv run arena register "Team Name" sim   # a simulator key
```

`arena register` exists for the simulator only: it hands out its own keys, which work nowhere
else. The arena's key comes from `/apply` (step 1).

`arena-sim` speaks the arena's public API exactly - paths, fields, statuses, error codes, limits,
the 60-second rule, quote PDFs and cost-breakdown XLSX files in the arena's format, RFQs with
parallel threads, leaderboard and replay JSON - with three example cases (`case:S01`-`S03`). Point
your agent at it to get the plumbing right without a network or a rate limit to worry about.
`--no-clock` switches the 60-second rule off for trying it by hand (above); without it the clock
runs, as on the arena. The first line it prints says which.

Its supplier is a deliberately plain script and **not** how the arena's suppliers behave: it opens
10 % above your current price, concedes a fixed 2 % per term sheet down to 90 %, agrees when you
meet its price, sends a final offer from round 5 and walks if you push after that; cited data is
only checked for existence. **The simulator teaches the contract; the real suppliers think for
themselves** - practise against them in the hosted arena and its sandbox (`--set sandbox`). We
don't hand out our suppliers: for a local opponent, build your own supplier simulator from the
public data - how would a foundry owner with a full order book answer your e-mail?
`starter-kit/Dockerfile` runs the simulator as a container. `uv run pytest` runs the kit's contract
tests against it; set `ARENA_TEST_URL` and `ARENA_TEST_KEY` to run them against a hosted arena too.

## MCP server over the data

A local, read-only MCP server (stdio) lets an MCP-capable agent or chat client explore the data
package itself. Six tools: `list_tables`, `query` (SELECT only, max 200 rows), `lookup` (the fact
behind a citable ID), `list_ids` (e.g. every month of one index series), `read_document`,
`get_case`.

```bash
uv run arena mcp --data /path/to/data/package   # speaks MCP on stdin/stdout
```

Add it to a client, e.g. Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add arena-data -- uv run --directory /path/to/starter-kit arena mcp --data /path/to/data/package
```

or any client with an `mcpServers` config:

```json
{"mcpServers": {"arena-data": {"command": "uv", "args": ["run", "--directory", "/path/to/starter-kit",
  "arena", "mcp", "--data", "/path/to/data/package"]}}}
```

## Good to know

- **60 s per message**, per thread. A late message counts as a timeout (your last offer repeated);
  `play()` reads the supplier's answer and goes on.
- **Invalid messages cost nothing**: `422` and no round used. `409` means the thread or case has
  ended, or you were late.
- **Your key is your team's.** Keep `.env` out of git.
- Tests: `uv run pytest`. Lint: `uv run ruff check .`

Where your team stands:

`practice`: sessions used and left in the rolling 24 hours, and when the oldest of them ages out
(the next one frees up); `best`: your best score per hosted practice case.

| Set | Cases | Replay |
|---|---|---|
| `practice` | all practice case files, to study; the **10 hosted** ones carry `"hosted": true` and can be played any time within your quota (a session on another is `403 "case:P06 is not hosted for practice"`); your best score per hosted case counts | right after the case |
| `sandbox` | `case:D01` (a price increase) and `case:D02` (an RFQ with two suppliers): three demo suppliers to try things on; no leaderboard | right after the case |
| `final` | the hidden cases (`"set": "hidden"`), wave by wave - see [Live Final](#live-final-in-waves); `403` before the first wave | after the final |

The replay is the same team view in every set: the e-mails as sent, terms, statuses, claim
results, the supplier's reasons in words and the score - as a real supplier would tell you. No rule
names, no internal parameters, none of the supplier's hidden figures (shown as `…`).

### `POST /v1/sessions`

`{"case_id": "case:P01"}` opens a case. Every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once (round 0);
from now on the 60-second clock runs per thread.

| Response field | |
|---|---|
| `session_id` | use in all further calls |
| `case` | the case file |
| `threads` | `{supplier_id: [opening message]}` - each supplier's quote e-mail, quote PDF attached |
| `opening` | the same quotes in the structured form of the `/moves` path |

Practice: your best score per case counts; at most 10 sessions open at a time (`429`).
**Quota: 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours.** Every practice session start
answers with the header `X-Practice-Remaining: <sessions left>`. At the limit: `429` with a detail
starting `practice limit:` that names `resets_at`, `X-Practice-Remaining: 0` and no `Retry-After` -
retrying does not help before then. Sandbox and final sessions do not count. Final: one session per team and case; a second is a `409` naming the running session -
pick it up again with `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}` and `GET …/threads/{supplier_id}`.

### `POST /v1/sessions/{sid}/threads/{supplier_id}/messages`

Body `{"message": Message}` (see [Messages](#messages)). Returns the supplier's reply, a Message.
With an `action`, it closes the case and returns the [result](#result-trace-and-back-office):
`{"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": "offer:…"}` takes that supplier's standing term sheet;
`{"type": "walk_away"}` ends the case without a deal.

A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**; its time never counts against your 60
seconds. Use an HTTP timeout of at least 180 s (the kit uses 180).

`422`: invalid message - nothing happens, no round is used (e.g. a term sheet without every
negotiable field, a value outside the allowed options, an unknown or stale `term_sheet_id`, more
than 3 term sheets). `409`: the thread or session has ended (in the final also at the wave's cap),
you reached the round limit (you may still accept), or your message came too late - it counted
as a timeout; `GET` the thread for the supplier's answer.

### `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}/threads/{supplier_id}`

The thread: `supplier_id`, `offer_id` (its standing term sheet), `status`, `closed` (why the thread
ended, else null), `messages` (all e-mails, both directions, in order; yours carry `"from":
"buyer"`), `timeouts` (the supplier's answers to your late moves). Enough to pick a case up again
after a crash.

### `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}/attachments/{attachment_id}`

The file of a supplier attachment (`application/pdf`, xlsx, ...), rendered from the supplier's
data. See [Documents](#documents).

### `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}`

The session state: `session_id`, `case_id`, `set`, `status` (`open` | `ended`), `end_reason`
(`accepted`, `walked_away`, `no_deal`, `timeout`, `wave_cap`, `window_closed`), `rounds`, `opening`, `threads`
(per supplier: `offer_id`, `status`, `offers`, `closed`, `seconds_left`) and, after the end,
`result` and `replay_url`.

### `GET /v1/sessions/{sid}/backoffice`

The supplier's roles talking internally (who asked whom, approvals, documents attached), in the
same team view: their words, without hidden figures or internal names. Only after the case has
ended - in the final after the final; before that `403`.

### Lists and boards

- `GET /health` - is the arena up? No key needed.
- `GET /v1/data` - the data downloads, no key needed: `{"package": {"url": "/v1/data/package.zip"},
  "release-sunday": {"public": false, "at": "2026-10-11T06:00:00+00:00"}}`. Once the Sunday
  release is public it carries `"url": "/v1/data/release-sunday.zip"` - new news, letters and a
  memo, with their own `facts.json` (new IDs only; package v1 stays as it is). Hidden cases may
  cite them; practice cases stay on package v1.

- `GET /v1/sessions?set=practice|sandbox|final` - your sessions: `session_id`, `case_id`, `status`,
  `end_reason`, `deal`, `score`, `rounds`, `created_at`.
- `GET /v1/leaderboard?set=practice|final` (JSON), `GET /leaderboard` (HTML screen) - no key
  needed. Practice: `total` = the mean of your best score per hosted case × 100 (cases not played
  count 0). Final: hidden cases only, live, as **points so far**:
  ```json
  {"set": "final", "cases": 6,
   "teams": [{"team_name": "Haggle Hounds", "played": 6, "deals": 6, "rounds": 21,
              "waves": {"1": 37.0, "2": 40.8}, "total": 77.8, "rank": 1,
              "saved_eur": 48210, "saved_eur_waves": {"1": 30115, "2": 18095}}],
   "waves": [{"n": 1, "theme": "Opening", "running": false, "closed": true, "seconds_left": 0}, …]}
  ```
  Per team, `waves` holds each started wave's score: the mean of its case scores × 100, 0-100, one
  decimal (a case you did not play scores your alternative once its wave has closed). `total` is
  the sum of those wave columns as shown - your points so far, up to 500 after five waves. Ranked by
  `total`; an exact tie goes to more `deals`, then fewer `rounds`. `cases` counts the cases of the
  waves started so far. **€ saved** (`saved_eur`, whole euros, per started wave in `saved_eur_waves`)
  is a side number and does not rank: per ended session `C_open − C_end`, where `C_end` is `c_deal`,
  or `c_alt` without a deal (0 if the case has no alternative) - money saved against the cheapest
  opening offer, over the case's horizon (`horizon_years`, 1-2 years), the same C as
  the score. It can be negative (a deal or an alternative dearer than the opening offer); a case
  you did not play saves nothing, nor does a deal that breaks a must-have (it scores 0). In the final the feed's `deal` and `no_deal` events carry it too.
  During the Live Final your agent must not read the leaderboard, the results, the screen or the
  event feed (`/v1/events`, `/v1/events/stream`, `/screen`, `/v1/screen`, `/v1/results`, `/results`)
  - they are for people.
- `GET /v1/results` (JSON), `GET /results` (page) - no key needed: the final's standings for people,
  every team: the final leaderboard above plus `"replays": true` once the final is closed. Before
  the first wave: no teams, nothing about the plan. `GET /v1/results/{team_name}` - one team's cases
  of the **started** waves: per wave `n`, `theme`, `running`, `closed`, `points`, `saved_eur` and
  `cases` - `case_id`, `title`, `type`, `suppliers` (names), `status` (`not started`, `in play`,
  `deal`, `no deal`; `not played` once its wave has closed - it scores your alternative), `end_reason`,
  `score`, `saved_eur`, `rounds`, and after the final `replay_url`. Both cached for 5 seconds.
- `GET /live` - the build page, no key needed (Sat 10:00 - Sun 12:00): every team's quota use,
  practice records and highlights.
- `GET /replay/{sid}` (link in the session's `replay_url`): a finished negotiation step by step -
  every e-mail and the supplier's reasons for each move in words, the same view in every set.
  Play, read the replay, improve, play again: that is the learning loop. Final: after the final,
  for everyone - the results page links each final session's replay then.

### The structured path

For agents that skip prose: `POST /v1/sessions/{sid}/moves` with `{"supplier_id": …, "move":
{"type": "offer", "offer_id": "<standing offer>", "terms": {…}, "claims": [{"type", "refs",
"asserted"}], "text": "≤ 800 chars"}}` returns a structured supplier move; `POST …/accept
{"offer_id"}` and `POST …/walk_away` close. Same supplier, same rules; claims are typed explicitly
(see [What counts](#what-counts)) instead of read from the message.
